opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the ingredients are finally coming together at the same time. If you look back at language models, scaling laws didn't appear out of nowhere. They showed up once three things were in place: a unified architecture, the Transformer; a massive and fairly homogeneous data source, the internet; and enough compute to run experiments across several orders of magnitude. Once you had all three, you could plot the curves and see the regularities.

For embodied intelligence, the bottleneck has always been data. A robot can't just crawl the web. Every trajectory has to be collected in the physical world, through teleoperation, real deployments, or simulation that's good enough to transfer. For a long time, each lab had its own robot, its own data format, and its own task setup, so you couldn't pool anything. Every dataset was a small island.

What's changed in the last year or two is that this is starting to converge. Hardware is becoming more standardized and much cheaper, so you can actually deploy hundreds or thousands of units instead of five. People are building data collection pipelines at real scale, almost like factories. And on the model side, vision-language-action models let us inherit a lot of world knowledge from pretrained vision and language models, so the robot data only has to teach the "action" part, not everything from scratch.

So when I say one or two years, I don't mean we'll have a general-purpose robot by then. I mean we'll probably have enough data, at enough diversity, across a consistent enough setup, to run clean experiments and see whether performance improves predictably as you scale data, model size, and compute. Some early signals already point that way. Cross-embodiment training, for example, tends to help rather than hurt, which is a good sign that there's a shared structure to learn.

There are real open questions, of course. What's the right unit of data: hours, episodes, tasks, or environments? How much can simulation substitute for real-world data? And the curve might turn out to be steeper or flatter than in language. But I think the question of whether a scaling law exists is going to get answered empirically pretty soon, and that by itself would change how the whole field invests and plans.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd frame it this way: the reason I'm fairly confident we'll see something like a Scaling Law in embodied intelligence within one or two years is that the ingredients are converging much faster than people outside the field realize.

Think about what happened with language models. The Scaling Law didn't appear out of nowhere. It appeared when three things lined up: a unified architecture, a huge pool of relatively cheap data, and a training objective that let you pour compute in and get predictable returns. For a long time robotics had none of those. Every lab had its own robot, its own sensors, its own task-specific pipeline. You couldn't aggregate anything, so you couldn't scale anything.

What's changed is that all three are now within reach. On architecture, the field has largely converged on the vision-language-action paradigm, where you take a pretrained multimodal model and attach an action head. That gives everyone a shared starting point and lets robots inherit the world knowledge already compressed into large models. On data, we finally have multiple channels that can be combined: teleoperation data from real robots, which is high quality but expensive; simulation and synthetic data, which is cheap and increasingly realistic; and large volumes of human video, which is noisy but essentially unlimited. Cross-embodiment training, where one model learns from many different robot bodies, means that data from different labs and hardware is no longer wasted. And on the compute side, we're just borrowing the entire infrastructure the LLM wave built.

So my argument is that for the first time, you can actually run the experiment. You can hold architecture fixed, vary data and parameters by orders of magnitude, and measure whether generalization on unseen tasks improves smoothly. Early results from several groups already show that curve bending the right way. It's not yet as clean as the language model curves, but it's starting to look like a law rather than a lucky result.

I'd add one caveat. "Scaling Law" in embodied intelligence probably won't look exactly like the language version. The bottleneck is not compute, it's data, and physical interaction data has a real-world cost. So the law we find may be a law about data efficiency as much as raw scale. But the key point is that we'll be able to say: if I invest this much more data and compute, I get roughly this much more capability. Once an industry has that kind of predictability, capital and talent flow in, and the whole thing accelerates. That's why I think the next one to two years are the window where it becomes visible.

astra-6.text:
I think one or two years is a plausible window because embodied intelligence is starting to become something we can study systematically at scale. But I’d distinguish finding a scaling law from solving robotics. Finding a scaling law means showing that, as you increase data, model capacity, and training compute, performance improves in a reasonably predictable way.

The key question is what we should scale. With robots, simply collecting more hours of the same movement may not help very much. You need diversity: different objects, environments, tasks, and interactions. You also need a way to measure whether a model can handle situations it hasn’t seen before, rather than just repeat what it learned.

Why might this happen within one or two years? Because we can start testing those relationships without waiting for a universally capable robot. If we train comparable models on progressively larger and more diverse datasets, and evaluate them on consistent tasks, we can see whether a stable pattern emerges. Pretrained models, simulation, and real-world interaction data give us several ways to run those experiments.

So that’s the basis for my optimism. It’s a hypothesis, not a guarantee. The decisive result would be that the trend lets us predict the performance of the next, larger model—and that the prediction holds on new tasks in the physical world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a reasonable chance, though I wouldn’t treat one or two years as a certainty. The key is whether we can establish a repeatable relationship between the resources we put in—data, compute, and model capacity—and a robot’s ability to complete tasks in the physical world.

That has been difficult because robotics data is fragmented. Different robots have different bodies, sensors, and action spaces, and each lab tests on different tasks. If you double the data but change everything else, it’s hard to tell what actually improved.

What makes me optimistic is that we can start to organize this as a more systematic experiment: use a common training framework, vary the amount and diversity of experience, and evaluate on tasks the model hasn’t seen. You don’t need to solve every robotics problem to discover a scaling relationship. You need a sufficiently consistent setup and enough experiments across different scales.

The distinction I’d make is between finding a scaling law and achieving general-purpose robots. Within one or two years, we may see convincing evidence that more of the right kind of data and compute produces predictable improvements. Turning that into reliable performance in an open-ended physical environment could take much longer.
